nary_nodes.label: English Language Bill passed
evidence: Lawmakers in New Zealand have passed a bill to make English one of the country’s official languages.
The bill — campaigned for by the nationalist New Zealand First party, part of the coalition government — passed its third reading in the House of Representatives on Thursday.
nary_nodes.type_definition: The event of a law or regulation being passed.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event fits; minting a new event type.

nary_nodes.label: Move widely ridiculed
evidence: The move was widely ridiculed in the Pacific Rim nation, where English is already widely used, including in courts and parliament.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event of mocking or deriding something.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event fits; minting a new event type.

nary_nodes.label: Paul's speech
evidence: In a video of a speech from that reading that has been viewed more than six million times on Instagram, Tamatha Paul, a member of New Zealand’s left-wing Green party, condemned the move as a waste of time, saying the “snowflake” government “see te reo Māori and they shiver in their boots.”
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where a record is awarded.
nary_nodes.type_justification: A speech is an event, and the example is a speech.

nary_nodes.label: Māori language decline
evidence: The education system established by the colonial government aimed to assimilate Māori into the burgeoning new society by discouraging the use of the native language, leading to a widespread decline in its use.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event of a historical decline in something.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event fits; minting a new event type.

nary_nodes.label: Māori language revival
evidence: But a campaign by Māori to revive the language in the early 1970s led to the establishment of the first bilingual schools, and to te reo Māori being made an official language in the 1980s.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event of a campaign to revive something.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event fits; minting a new event type.

nary_nodes.label: Parliamentary debate
evidence: During the debate, Labour MP Camilla Belich mockingly mused, “I wondered if they might want to legislate for the changing of the seasons?”
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where a record is awarded.
nary_nodes.type_justification: A debate is an event, and the example is a debate.

nary_nodes.label: Justice Committee report
evidence: In a report presented to the House in June, the country’s Justice Committee said it received written submissions from 1,601 people and groups regarding the bill, and almost two-thirds of these opposed it.
nary_nodes.type_justification: A report presentation is a publication event, and the example is a report.

nary_nodes.label: Costello defends bill
evidence: Casey Costello, a member of the New Zealand First party, was among those who defended the move in parliament during the third reading.
She said the purpose of the “short, straightforward bill” is to “recognize in legislation what has long been assumed in New Zealand. Namely, that English is an official language of our country.”
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event fits; minting a new event type.

nary_nodes.label: Paul criticizes bill
evidence: Tamatha Paul, a member of New Zealand’s left-wing Green party, condemned the move as a waste of time, saying the “snowflake” government “see te reo Māori and they shiver in their boots.”
“We had to march our asses to parliament demanding that the indigenous first language of this country be recognized and not beaten out of the mouths of its native speakers,” Paul said.

nary_nodes.label: Belich mocks bill
evidence: During the debate, Labour MP Camilla Belich mockingly mused, “I wondered if they might want to legislate for the changing of the seasons?”

nary_nodes.label: Opponents argue against bill
evidence: According to the report, opponents of the move argued that making English an official language would be “an unnecessary use of resources,” create “unnecessary division within society,” and would be “undermining the two other official languages” and their legislation, which gave those minority languages stronger rights and supported their use in legal proceedings.

nary_nodes.label: Supporters argue for bill
evidence: Those in support of the bill said the legislation would clarify the long-accepted status of English and, since the bill would not introduce any new rights for the language, would cause little harm.

nary_nodes.label: Costello defends bill
evidence: She said the purpose of the “short, straightforward bill” is to “recognize in legislation what has long been assumed in New Zealand. Namely, that English is an official language of our country.”

“Despite what has been claimed across this House, this bill is important and far from the claimed ‘waste of time,’” Costello added, before going on to say, “It is not trivial, unnecessary or a distraction to this House in a democracy to deliver for those who elected us to this House.”
